content: The World Health Organization (WHO) and the relevant experts conducted a thorough evaluation of potential candidates for the Guideline Development Group (GDG). Each candidate was required to submit a completed Declaration of Interests (DOI) form and a curriculum vitae (CV). Additionally, an internet search was performed to identify any public controversies or interests that could potentially compromise the candidate’s objectivity or the integrity of the WHO. Members of the steering committee reviewed the CVs, DOI forms, and internet findings to assess whether any actual or perceived conflicts of interest (COI) existed. If conflicts were identified, the committee determined whether a management plan was necessary. The evaluation process adhered to the WHO Guidelines for Declaration of Interests for experts and the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development (2nd edition). Both financial and non-financial interests were considered. A significant conflict of interest was defined as including intellectual bias (e.g., when an individual has publicly taken a position on an issue under review, potentially affecting their objectivity), involvement in research or publication related to the issue under review, or financial interests exceeding USD 5,000. Developers of diagnostic assays were automatically excluded from policy development processes due to inherent conflicts of interest. Once it was determined that no conflict of interest existed or that any identified conflicts could be appropriately managed, the candidate’s name and a brief biography were published on the WHO website for at least 14 days prior to the meeting to allow for public notice and comment. During the meeting, the WHO steering committee summarized the DOI statements for all GDG members. Individuals with intellectual or research involvement in the subject matter were invited as technical resource persons to provide input and answer technical questions. However, these individuals did not participate in the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) process and were excluded from group discussions when recommendations were being developed. The WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis (TB) diagnostics included a detailed review of conflicts of interest for GDG and External Review Group (ERG) members. For example, some members declared no conflicts of interest, while others disclosed financial or research-related interests. In cases where significant conflicts of interest were identified, such as financial support from diagnostic companies or involvement in related research, the individuals were excluded from deliberations on specific topics to ensure impartiality. The WHO guidelines emphasize transparency and rigorous conflict of interest management to maintain the integrity of the guideline development process. This includes publishing DOI summaries, consulting with the WHO Ethics Team, and implementing management plans when necessary. The process ensures that both financial and intellectual biases are addressed to uphold the credibility of global health policy recommendations.
